title: Customer success
brief_markdown:
The order form is not the finish line. The moment Marcus signs, a clock starts: the 50%-off beta year runs out, and whether he renews at full price is decided in the first fourteen days, not in month eleven. Customer success is keeping the promise the narrative made in Module 2: fewer feedback rounds, creators who get better video over video, winners you can reproduce on purpose. This module is where you deliver it, measure it, and show it back until renewal is a formality.

### Why it matters more now than later
Three things hang on the first five or six beta customers. The renewal. Expansion: more brands under Dana's agency, more creators in Marcus's programme, Sofia's German launch. And proof: the testimonial, the number on the proof slide, the reference call that makes the next five sales easier. None of that happens to a customer who signed, got a Discord invite and went quiet. The window is short: a new customer gives you attention for a couple of weeks while the purchase still feels like a decision they are proud of; reviving a stalled account later is a second, harder sale.

### Define success before anyone logs in
Success is the KPI from the narrative, in the customer's unit, per stakeholder. For a brand like Marcus: hook rate on round-two videos or GMV per approved video; for his TikTok Shop manager: hours of feedback per week. For an agency like Dana: feedback rounds per video, approved videos per week, a quality story she can show clients. Pick one metric per segment, and a **time to first value**: the first moment the customer sees Myda do something they could not, probably a creator re-shooting after a Myda note and the second version being visibly better. Aim for inside seven days. Write the metric down at kickoff in the customer's words and email it back the same day.

### Onboarding: the first fourteen days
Implementation for Myda is short, but it is not "send the invite". Value needs three preconditions: the brief is loaded, the creators are in the loop (a Discord channel or an email list), and the first videos are in. Before the kickoff, reread the close plan and the CRM: who sponsored the deal (Marcus), who will use it daily (his manager), what they bought for. Do the pre-work yourself: set up the workspace, load their brief, pull three of their creators' public videos and run feedback on them, so the call opens with their content rather than a tour.

The kickoff, 45 minutes, one user at a time, never a group (in a group nobody is accountable). Agenda: rediscovery ("you bought because X; still true?", and if the answer surprises you, fix it now, not in month three); setup (login, brief in, creator channel connected, Myda bookmarked; if that is fiddly, split off a 15-minute setup call first); then the user drives and you coach: she runs the first video through, reads the feedback, sends the first note to a creator. Then homework with numbers: ten videos through Myda and notes to five creators by day 7. Say out loud that you will be watching usage and reporting to Marcus; that alone creates a tailwind. Confirm the support contact, send the recording afterwards, and do not hang up until the day-7 call is on both calendars.

Day 3: look at usage, not your inbox; no videos in, message the same day. Day 7: short call, review the homework, name the first result, clear snags. Day 14: an "operational" email to the sponsor with what happened and the metric so far. Missed kickoff? Reschedule hard. User leaves? Onboard the replacement as a new customer. And remember each person's "what's in it for me": the manager wants to look like a better content lead; Marcus wants the number.

### Support that does not leak
One channel the customer already lives in, a response promise you can keep (acknowledge within the hour in working hours, fix or workaround within a day), and a named founder on duty. When something breaks, take the blame, fix it, and close the thread only when the user confirms it is fixed. The second time a question arrives, write the answer once. Tag every issue by product area; once a month engineering gets the list ranked by frequency, remembering the ten silent users behind every one who complained. Never promise a customer a date on his behalf.

### Watch usage before they complain
You can see the precursors of value in the product: videos uploaded per week, notes sent, creators who replied, round-two videos that came back. The signals that predict churn: no videos for seven days, feedback generated but never sent, no creator ever re-shooting, the user changing, the sponsor no longer opening your emails. Each gets a specific response, framed as "I want you to get the result you bought for", never "you're not using it". Usually it is competing priorities, and you can be the manager: offer to block a Tuesday slot. Spend your time on the C+ accounts; the A's are fine, and for the F's go to the sponsor, respectfully, and ask for a different user.

### Show the value back
Customers are busy and forget why they bought. Weekly in the beta, monthly after, a success review with the sponsor: the shared goal restated, the metric before and after, who is using it and who is not with the cost of the gap, and a proposed plan. When the numbers are good, this is where you ask: a case study, an intro to a peer, more brands or seats. When they are not, do not ask; fix. Summarise the actions in an email and log every outcome in the CRM with a date.

### Renewal
Renewing at full price after a half-price year is a doubling; it only feels like a no-brainer if the value was documented all year. Auto-renew goes in the Module 8 order form. Last success review three months before term end, renewal call six weeks out with the whole-term numbers, then ask for the business explicitly. Spend half that call on their goals for next year; that is where expansion lives. If there is a snag, extend a month free rather than lose the account.

### Feed it back
Customer success feeds product (ranked tags), pipeline (a champion who changes jobs is a warm lead; a happy sponsor is a reference call) and marketing (every proof number). Block the calendar for it the day a deal closes, and track kickoffs and reviews in the CRM like pipeline stages: "closed won, no kickoff yet" should be a query you can run.

### This week
Pick the metric per segment. Write the kickoff agenda and run it with the first beta customer. Ask engineering for the usage view. Set the support channel and the response promise. Put every customer's day-7, day-14, monthly and renewal dates in the calendar now.

### What you build in this module
The customer success plan: the metric per segment, the 14-day onboarding with kickoff agenda and homework, the churn signals and the response to each, the check-in cadence, the support rules, the expansion and referral asks, the renewal timeline against the beta term, and the customer health table you review together every week.

### Drill
Marcus, thirty days in, usage stalled, half-wondering whether to pause. Diagnose before you propose, agree a metric, leave with an adoption plan and a date.

### Where this leaves you
You now own the whole motion end to end: narrative, materials, ICP, outreach, inbound, pitch, close and success plan, each feeding the next. Revisit the narrative and the ICP monthly against what customers actually said, and the pricing whenever nobody blinks. The artifacts are hypotheses the market keeps editing; the CRM log is where the edits come from.

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s customer success plan, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move on. Pull the promised KPIs and the "who has it" roles from the company artifact's Narrative section, and the pilot scope, owner, start date and "first result" date from the closing artifact's close plan; do not re-litigate them here. The beta term (50% off for one year, 3-week beta with 2 feedback sessions) comes from the company artifact.

1. **Definition of a successful customer.** One metric per segment (agency, brand), in the customer's unit, with the before-value you capture at kickoff and the target. Then time to first value: the first observable moment {{company}} did something they could not, and the day by which it must happen. Push back on metrics {{company}} cannot see or the customer does not already track.
2. **Onboarding, days 0 to 14.** Pre-work the founders do before kickoff (workspace, brief loaded, three of the customer's creator videos pulled and run). Kickoff agenda for a 45-minute call: rediscovery line, setup checklist, the three videos the user runs herself, the first creator note she sends, homework with numbers for day 7, support contact, recording sent, next call booked before hanging up. Who at the customer must be on it (sponsor and daily user, named by role per segment) and why groups are refused. The creator-feedback loop set-up: Discord or email, who invites the creators, what the creators are told. Day-3 and day-7 touches with their trigger and the message. Day-14 "operational" email to the sponsor. What engineering needs to be told at each deal close (accounts, users, channel, the usage signals he must expose).
3. **Usage signals and responses.** A table: signal, threshold, what it predicts, who acts, the exact first message. Minimum: no videos in 7 days; feedback generated but not sent; no round-two video from any creator in 14 days; the daily user changed; the sponsor stopped replying. Include the A / C+ / F triage rule and when to go to the sponsor.
4. **Check-in cadence.** Weekly 20-minute call during the beta, monthly success review after. Agenda for each, the five questions asked every time (rediscovery, metric before/after, who is using it and who is not, what broke, what next), who attends, and the follow-up email that summarises actions.
5. **Support rules.** Channel, acknowledgement time, resolution time, who is on duty (rotation between {{founder_1}} and {{founder_2}}), the rule for closing a thread, when a question becomes a written note, how issues are tagged, and the monthly feedback list to engineering. Explicit rule: no dates promised to customers.
6. **Expansion and referral playbook.** For each ask (case study, testimonial quote, referral to a peer, reference call, more seats or brands, a new market), the trigger that makes it askable, who asks whom, and the exact wording of the ask in one or two sentences. Rule: never ask in a review where the numbers are bad.
7. **Renewal timeline.** Dates counted back from the end of the 50%-off beta year: final success review, renewal call, order form sent, and what the renewal call must show (the term-long metric, the goals for the next year). The sentence that asks for the renewal. The fallback if there is a snag (free extension, not a discount).
8. **Customer health table.** The table the founders review together every week: one row per customer with sponsor, daily user, metric before / now, videos this week, notes sent, creators re-shooting, last touch, next touch, health (green / amber / red), renewal date, owner. Seed it with every beta customer and pilot from the closing artifact's pipeline.

Standards to enforce on every section: each metric is one the customer already tracks or {{company}} can see in the product; every touch has an owner, a trigger and a date; every ask has exact wording a founder would say tomorrow; nothing in the plan requires engineering to ship something by a date. Push back on vague cadences ("check in regularly"), on metrics like "engagement", and on support promises the two founders cannot keep while also selling. Mark the artifact done only when all eight sections exist and the health table has a row for every current customer.

drill.scenario: Thirty days after Marcus signed (Module 8). His TikTok Shop manager ran four videos through {{company}} in week one and nothing since; the creator feedback loop was never set up, so no creator has received a note. The kickoff happened, the day-7 call was rescheduled twice and never held. Marcus is irritated, has not seen a number, and is half-wondering whether to pause. He tests you with 'my guy says he's too busy', 'what have we actually got out of this?', 'can we just pause until Q1?' and, if you get defensive, 'so what's the discount for a year we didn't use?'. Your goal: diagnose why adoption stalled with questions before proposing anything, restate the goal he bought for, agree one success metric and a timeframe, leave with an adoption plan (who does what by when, including the creator loop) and a date for the next check-in, and name when the renewal conversation happens. Do not offer a discount.
drill.buyer_opening: Honestly, I'm not sure we're getting anything out of this yet. My guy says he's too busy to use it, and I haven't seen a single number. Convince me we shouldn't just pause until Q1.

rows.criterion: Opened with rediscovery: restated the goal and the metric Marcus bought for in his own words, not with features or apologies
Diagnosed why adoption stalled with open questions (time, setup, the creator loop, the user) before proposing anything
Identified the daily user and the blocker by name or role, and treated the stalled user as a priorities problem to manage, not a character flaw
Agreed one success metric, its before-value and a timeframe that Marcus accepted out loud
Proposed a concrete adoption plan: numbered homework, the creator-feedback loop set up, who does what by when, and offered to do the set-up work himself
Asked for product feedback, recorded the gaps without arguing, and promised no delivery dates
Handled the pause threat and the discount probe without getting defensive and without discounting: named the opportunity cost of pausing and offered time, not money
Booked the next check-in with a date before the call ended and named when the renewal conversation happens against the beta term

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: fix the onboarding plan and the usage-signal responses in the success artifact before repeating with the same persona. Carry forward the weakest row as the standing fix; add every reason Marcus gave for the stall to the signals table.
